payload.MatterTitle: C/S Amending Huning Highland Boundary Map and Zoning Map for Lots in the Boundary Expansion Area as Articulated (Griego)
payload.MatterEXText1:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\li120\b\f0\fs24 Summary.  \b0 This legislation has been submitted to partially implement the recommendations and provisions of the East Downtown (EDo) Master Plan.  The EDo Plan is a privately created and unadopted development proposal.   Other elements of the implementation effort are addressed in Bill Nos. R-04-146 and R-04-155 and within the EDo plan document itself.
\par \b\tab\b0 In specific, one provision of this bill calls for a portion of the EDo Master Plan area to be amended into the Downtown 2010 Sector Plan area.  This area is generally east of the railroad tracks, west of Broadway, and south of Central.  The exact boundaries are lots east from the railroad tracks to the north-south alley west of Broadway Boulevard, from Gold Avenue to Lead Avenue, excluding the properties owned by the Burlington Northern Santa Fe (BNSF) Railway and the Salvation Army.  This area is not within the current boundaries of the Huning Highland Sector Plan.  Portions of the Downtown 2010 Sector Plan currently do extend east of the railway tracks, to Broadway Blvd to the north of the proposed area.
\par \tab The second provision of Bill No. R-04-158 would amend the zoning of this area from M-1 to SU-3, with the Mixed Use District land use designator.  However, the O-3 zone, providing for unrestricted heights of office buildings, would not be included.
\par \tab\b Fiscal Impact.  \b0 Adoption of this legislation will have no immediate impact on City revenues.  The Administration also reports no increase in City costs to implement the proposed legislation.  Should this legislation facilitate the redevelopment of the area there are likely to be impacts both in City revenues and also in City costs associated with the reuse (residential, retail, commercial) of the area.
\par \b\tab Comment.\b0   The adoption of this Resolution would make it simpler administratively to redevelop this area consistent with the type of mixed-use (residential, retail, commercial, etc) plan proposed in the EDo Master Plan.  
\par \pard\fi600\li120 Including the property in the Downtown 2010 Sector Plan, as was originally proposed in the Plan, would classify this area as "Warehouse".  In the Warehouse area the following uses are identified as "Permitted": ground floor residential, above ground residential, retail/services, office/institutional, warehouse/wholesale, and manufacturing (as allowed in the M-1 Zone).  Permitted uses with regard to new construction would be subject to review by the Planning Director/Review Team and, if approved, would proceed to building permit issuance.  The entire review and building permit issuance process was envisioned as 11 day to 24 days.  
\par Development would be subject to the design standards contained in the Downtown 2010 Plan regarding such elements as building set backs on the lot, build-to lines, massing, set-backs, parking, and so on.  
\par \b Question.
\par \pard\fi-360\li1080\b0 1.  Why wasn't this area included in the final adopted boundary of the Downtown 2010 Plan?
\par 2.  Why wasn't this area included in the Urban Conservation Overlay Zone proposed in the other EDo legislation?
\par \pard             3.     Why are the Burlington Northern and Salvation Army parcels excluded from this area?\f1\fs23 
\par }

payload.MatterTitle: F/S Amending a Portion of The Zoning Code, Section 14-16-2-22(B) ROA 1994, The SU-1 Special Use Zone, To Include Form Based Zones As A Special Use; Amending Chapter 14, Article 16, Part 3, ROA 1994, The General Regulations of The Zoning Code, To Add Form Based Zones That Prescribe Building Form, Frontage Type, Parking, Connectivity, Design, Signage and Lighting Standards, and That Describe Form Based Zones That Allow Mixed Use Development That Is Transit Oriented and Development That Is Oriented Toward Pedestrian Traffic (Benton)
payload.MatterEXText1:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 LUPZ 12/10/08 dls\b 
\par Summary:\b0   This ordinance replaces a similar previous ordinance which died on expiration one year after introduction.
\par \tab The ordinance is to allow Form Based Zones to be included in the list of options available in the City's Special Use (SU) zone as an option.  The zones will be added to the City's existing Zoning Code and will be available for use by application to the Environmental Planning Commission.
\par \tab These zones place an emphasis on form and design and allow mixed uses to occur.
\par \tab It is important to note that these zones will in no case be mandatory.  To acquire one of these zones for a property, an application for zone change would need to occur and go through the process required for any zone change.  If one or more of these zones were desired for a sector plan, the zone change and sector plan amendment would have to go to the Environmental Planning Commission, as well as the City Council for approval.
\par \f1\fs23 
\par }

payload.MatterTitle: Adopting an Infrastructure and Growth Plan Pursuant to ROA 1994 (Cadigan)

Repeal of The Nob Hill Sector Development Plan and Adoption of The Nob Hill Highland Sector Development Plan (NHHSDP) and Change of Zoning For Certain Properties Within The NHHSDP Boundary Area As Specified In Exhibit A (Heinrich)
payload.MatterEXText1:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\froman\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 LUPZ 2/28/07 ljm\b 
\par Summary:\b0    This bill adopts the Nob Hill Highland Sector Development Plan and rezones some properties within that Plan.  There is presently a sector plan in place for the Nob Hill area, but due to the extensive revisions proposed after a long public process of review and input, the existing plan is being repealed and a new plan will replace it.  
\par \tab The sector plan area is bounded on the west by Girard, Lomas on the North, San Mateo on the east and Zuni/Garfield on the south.  The new boundaries expand the old plan area to include an area around Highland High School, and will make the sector plan area consistent with the existing Central/Highland/Upper Nob Hill Metropolitan Redevelopment Area.  The EPC recommended approval of the new plan.  If the Council approves and adopts the proposed sector development plan, the existing moratorium will be terminated.
\par \b Fiscal Impact:  \b0 The fiscal impact analysis prepared by the Administration\b  \b0 indicates what capital funds are earmarked or available to implement projects listed in the plan as priorities.  The FIA also states that future funds will be needed to address Phase 2 (Central between Girard and Carlisle) and other priorities listed in the plan.  The FIA states that those funds will be requested through the City's CIP and from the State.  The cost estimate for pedestrian friendly streetscape and drainage improvements along Central is $3 to $3.5 million.  
\par \b Comments:   \b0 The public comment process for this plan was extensive and many issues were discussed.  One focus of the plan was to improve circulation along and across Central Avenue for pedestrian, bicycle and vehicle traffic.  The plan also sought to continue the business friendly nature of Central in the Nob Hill district and to increase opportunities for mixed uses, including residential uses.  The Planning Department, at the EPC's direction after its public hearing, addressed several key issues which are set forth in the record on pages 3 through 7:  building heights, solar access, standards for pedestrian facilities, residential zones in the commercial district, building facades that face residential areas, "green" buildings, wider sidewalks, sidewalk shading, historical designations, integration of a future streetcar system, neighborhood scale development at the intersection of Carlisle, Monte Vista and Lomas, and designating a portion of the plan area as "East Nob Hill".  The Planning Staff addressed the above issues and resolved to address other issues with additional city-wide ordinance revisions in the future.  The staff noted that a protest was filed by an owner of a drug store property regarding the plan's prohibition of drive-through windows in the CCR-1 zone (Community Commercial/Residential).  Planning staff point out that such a prohibition has existed in the existing plan's CCR zone since 1992 and a drive through window in that zone would not be consistent with the goal of the plan to increase walkability in that section of the plan area.  
\par \b Questions:\b0\tab Is the Legal Department satisfied that the requirements of R-270-1980 for zone map amendments have been met?\f1\fs23 
\par }

payload.MatterTitle: Adopting Land Use Assumptions Pursuant to the State Development Fees Act and ROA 1994 (Cadigan)
payload.MatterEXText1:
{\rtf1\ansi\deff0\deftab720{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss MS Sans Serif;}{\f1\froman\fcharset2 Symbol;}{\f2\fswiss\fprq2 Arial;}{\f3\froman Times New Roman;}}
{\colortbl\red0\green0\blue0;}
\deflang1033\pard\plain\f2\fs22\b Summary:  \plain\f2\fs22 This Ordinance adopts the Land Use Assumptions that provide the basis for the Growth Capital Improvement Program that is used in calculating development impact fees.  The Land Use Assumptions contain projections, by sub-area, of growth in population, housing and jobs over the periods 2000 \endash  2010 and 2010 \endash  2025.  The Growth Capital Improvement Program identifies the costs associated with providing the public infrastructure and services to accommodate that growth.  These costs are apportioned to new development in the form of impact fees.\plain\f2\fs22\b 
\par \plain\f2\fs22 
\par \plain\f2\fs22\b Fiscal Impact:\plain\f2\fs22   None, for adopting the Land Use Assumptions.  \plain\f2\fs22\b 
\par \plain\f2\fs22 
\par \plain\f2\fs22\b Comments:  \plain\f2\fs22 The NM Development Fees Act and the legislation adopting the Planned Growth Strategy require that Land Use Assumptions be adopted by the Council and that the Council be advised and assisted in that action by the Impact Fee Committee.  The Impact Fee Committee voted to recommend the Land Use Assumptions be adopted and a letter conveying that recommendation is included in the bill packet.
\par 
\par \plain\f2\fs22\b Questions:\plain\f2\fs22   \plain\f2\fs22\b 
\par \pard\li720\fi-360\plain\f2\fs22 1.\tab What is the relationship between these Land Use Assumptions and the Infrastructure and Growth Plan adopted by the Council in October 2003?
\par 2.\tab What is the length of time for which the Land Use Assumptions hold?
\par \pard\plain\f3\fs23 
\par }

F/S Amending Section 14-14-5-3 ROA 1994, A Portion of The Subdivision Ordinance, To Require Certain Notice and Approval Prior To The Granting of An Extension of a Subdivision Improvements Agreement (Cadigan)
payload.MatterEXText1:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}{\f2\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\fs24 LUPZ 2/11/09 btt\f1\fs23 
\par \b\f2\fs24 Summary: \b0 The City's Subdivision Ordinance provides that a developer is responsible to provide the infrastructure necessary to support a proposed development. The developer has the option of actually constructing that infrastructure prior to development or entering into a contract with the City whereby the developer agrees to the future construction of the required infrastructure. The contract which obligates the developer to construct the infrastructure at a future date is a Subdivision Improvements Agreement ("SIA"). The developer provides a financial guarantee at the time the SIA is entered into. If the work required to be performed under the SIA is not completed the City can use the financial guarantee to construct the infrastructure itself.
\par \tab By ordinance, the maximum length of time that can be allowed to complete infrastructure under an SIA is two years. \'a7 14-14-5-3. The time period can be extended by the DRB "for good cause which shall be determined in the manner established in the Development Process Manual." \ul Id\ulnone .
\par \tab This bill requires that prior to any SIA extension that the Department of Municipal Development must indicate in writing that the Department has reviewed and agrees to such an extension and the applicant must demonstrate that the City's Air Quality Division has reviewed the request.  
\par \tab Finally, under the bill, any request for an extension longer than six months must be approved by the City Council.
\par \b Comments: \b0 The Development Process Manual provides that the DRB shall not approve an SIA extension: "unless it makes findings, based upon the evidence presented to it at a public meeting, that:
\par \pard\li360\tab 1. The extension would not be injurious to the public safety, health or welfare, or to adjacent property, the neighborhood or the community; and
\par \tab 2. The extension will not conflict significantly with the goals and provisions of any City, County, or AMAFCA adopted plan or policy, the applicable zoning ordinance, or any other City Ordinances; and
\par \tab 3. The extension will not hinder future planning, public right-of-way acquisition, or the financing of construction of public infrastructure improvements."
\par \pard With respect to the requirement that DMD and Air Quality affirmatively be shown to have reviewed and/or approved the extension the bill simply ensures that there has been communication with these divisions by the DRB. 
\par \tab The requirement that the City Council approve extensions of over six months ensures that lengthy extensions which have the potential to create extensive harm to the environment and the community are thoroughly reviewed.
\par \b EPC Recommends Against Approval: \b0 The EPC had no opposition to the required review by DMD and Air Quality but recommends against the requirement for City Council approval. The EPC found that this would amount to around 40 or more extensions being sent to the City Council each year for approval. The additional delay and added bureaucratic layer were not seen as justified. In discussion at the EPC, it was believed that excessive dust from long delayed projects was probably the primary motivation behind the bill. However, where such problems exist it was stated that any DRB extension approval is appealable to the City Council.
\par \tab A concern was raised at the EPC about having the chair of the DRB be the staff person to make recommendations on this bill that would take away certain DRB authority. Other persons assigned to review ordinances for the EPC will often contact City Council staff to discuss the intent of a bill. Mr. Cloud testified to the EPC that he had no idea why Council approval of extensions was proposed and had clearly not sought to find out. 
\par \b Fiscal Impact: \b0 None 
\par \b Questions: \b0 Are Neighborhood Associations given notice of the hearings on these extensions so that concerns can be raised?\f1\fs23 
\par }

payload.MatterTitle: F/S Authorizing The Giving Of Notices For Bids For The Sale Of City Of Albuquerque, New Mexico General Obligation Bonds Consisting Of $102,850,000 General Obligation General Purpose Bonds, Series 2024A, And $9,000,000 General Obligation Storm Sewer Bonds, Series 2024B (Peña, by request)
payload.MatterEXText1:
CC 4/3/24 (MMM)
FGO 3/11/24 (mmm)

Summary: This resolution serves as the outline for the bid parameters and the schedule of a competitive bond sale consisting of $102,850,000 General Purpose General Obligation Bonds and $9,000,000 of Storm Sewer Bonds. Currently the schedule is for a competitive safe on April 3rd with the closing on or about April 24th, 2024. 
								2023 Election	2024 Sale
Public Safety 						$25,051,666 	$18,500,000
Citizens' Centers and Community Enhancement 	$35,880,001 	$19,050,000
Parks and Recreation 					$34,946,666 	$14,400,000
Energy/Water Conservation, Facilities and Equipment 	$24,155,000 	$12,200,000
Streets and Transportation 				$50,061,667 	$34,200,000
Museum, Cultural Facilities and Library 			$15,595,000 	$4,500,000
SUBTOTAL	 					$185,690,000 	$102,850,000
Storm Sewer 						$14,310,000 	$9,000,000
TOTAL 							$200,000,000 	$111,850,000
The maximum cost of issuing the new bonds is approximately $111,850,000, inclusive of CIP project funds, cost of issuance expenses and interest (determined at the time of the bond sale). Debt service will be covered by City property tax revenues, with the general fund bridging any shortfall.
Fiscal Impact: There will be a fiscal impact in FY ’25 and FY ’26 until FY ’40 for the payment of the debt service.
Comments: It is the policy of the City of Albuquerque not to issue new bonds until old bonds are paid off, keeping our mil rate level every year.
This funding will go towards building capital improvements across the City.

CC 12/16/24 (jc)

Brief Summary: O-96 was introduced on December 4, 2023, so pursuant to the City Council Rules of Procedure, it has “died on expiration.”

Council Rules of Procedure Section 6(A)(9) provides that: 

Any bill which is not adopted by the City Council within one year from the date of its introduction shall be deemed to have "Died on Expiration," and no further action shall be taken by the Council or its committees on the bill. Bills which are deemed "Died on Expiration" may be reintroduced under a new bill number pursuant to the provisions of subsections (1) through (8) of this section.

FGO 5/13/24 (jgr)

Summary:	This bill proposes to create a new ordinance that would create an Environmental Justice Air Quality Permit program that would be administered by the City’s Environmental Health Department. This new permit requirement would apply to “a person who intends to construct a new stationary source or modify an existing stationary source that is subject to permitting” under certain portions of the New Mexico Administrative Code. 
Mapping of Overburdened and Vulnerable Communities: 	
•	This Ordinance directs the Environmental Health Department to develop and publish on its website a map of Vulnerable and Overburdened Communities within 180 days of the enactment of this Ordinance. 
•	Then, the permitting requirements for Applicants will go into effect 180 calendar days after the map is published. 
•	Vulnerable and Overburdened Communities are areas where the public experiences heightened or maximum exposures that are likely to cause a higher risk of poor public health outcomes. 
•	The map will also include Adverse Environmental and Public Health Indicators that have a demonstrable nexus with air pollution, but these indicators will not be considered standards required to identify quantities and duration of specified air contaminants that constitute air pollution. 
•	For each Adverse Environmental and Public Health Indicator, the Department shall publish the justification, literature, data source(s), methodology, and additional resources supporting inclusion on the map. Information regarding the adverse environmental and public health indicators used by the Department shall be based on the latest scientific data. Localized data may be used when it is peer reviewed, and consistent with accepted scientific practices. 
•	Recognized Neighborhood Associations and Coalitions can also submit information about their community to be included with the map. 
•	This map will be updated following the US Census and notice will be provided by the Department following any updates to the map. 

Initial Screening Information & Pre-Application Environmental Justice Consultation:  	
•	After the map goes into effect, Applicants must contact EHD for an Environmental Justice Consultation to discuss whether the Applicant may locate the proposed source, in whole or in part, in a Vulnerable or Overburdened Community and what, if any, additional permitting requirements apply pursuant to this Ordinance.
•	EHD will provide the Applicant with initial screening information, including both a list of all Adverse Environmental and Public Health Indicators on the overall map and a list of the Indicators that are present in the Vulnerable or Overburdened Community in which the source will be located and any Communities within a half-mile radius around the source location.
•	The Applicant must review the initial screening information and attend the Environmental Justice Consultation before moving on to the next steps in the permitting process. EHD shall not waive the Environmental Justice Consultation requirement. 

Environmental Justice Assessment Report:	
•	An Applicant must conduct an environmental justice assessment and document its findings in an Environmental Assessment Report for the purposes of: providing the core information necessary to assess the existing Adverse Environmental and Public Health Indicators in a Vulnerable or Overburdened Community; document how the construction of a new stationary source or modification or relocation of an existing stationary source will impact those Adverse Environmental and Public Health Indicators; any measures the source proposes to address those impacts; document the nature of the community it proposes to locate in; assess the source’s impact on the community; and provide the community with information about the source to facilitate meaningful public outreach. 
•	The report shall include nineteen (19) components listed in the Ordinance, including: an executive summary; initial screening information; a description of the source and its purpose; compliance information; an assessment of the source’s impact on all Adverse Environmental and Public Health Indicators and mitigation steps the Applicant proposes to implement; zoning certifications; and a site plan, if applicable. 
•	EHD can provide resources to assist with preparation of the Report, and Applicants can submit their Reports to EHD for review and recommendations before moving on to the Enhanced Public Engagement portion of the permitting process. 
•	The Report must be updated by the Applicant following the Enhanced Public Engagement process. 

Enhanced Public Engagement – Public Notice & Public Information Meeting: 
•	Before submitting a final application to EHD, Applicants must comply with Enhanced Public Engagement requirements by providing notice to the public and potentially holding a Public Information Meeting. 
•	Applicants must provide public notice of the stationary source that the Applicant proposes to construct or modify, including contact information, a summary of the Environmental Justice Assessment Report, an invitation to provide public comment, and information about the circumstances in which a Public Information Meeting may be held, if there is “significant public interest.”
•	After giving notice, the Applicant must hold a Public Information Meeting if there is significant public interest. Public interest is significant when: five or more individuals request or petition for a meeting, an elected official or an elected representative of a Recognized Neighborhood Association or Coalition requests a meeting, or if the Applicant or EHD Director determines that public interest is significant.
•	If a Public Information Meeting is held, it must be properly noticed, should take place in the Vulnerable or Overburdened Community, be available in both in-person and virtual formats, be recorded or transcribed, and should be scheduled for at least one hour. All expenses for the meeting will be paid for by the Applicant.
•	At the meeting, the Applicant shall and the Applicant shall: (1) describe the source the Applicant proposes to construct or modify; (2) provide a detailed presentation on the Environmental Justice Assessment Report; (3) accept written and oral public comments, information, and questions; and (4) respond to comments and questions. 
•	As part of the Enhanced Public Engagement process, EHD may also impose additional Inclusive Community Resource requirements on the Applicant, to ensure that people with different abilities are able to fully participate in the permitting process and that information is accessible and reaches populations in Vulnerable or Overburdened communities.
•	Following the conclusion of the Enhanced Public Engagement process, the Applicant must update the Environmental Assessment Report before submitting a final application.

Application for Permit / EHD Review and Decision 
•	The Ordinance also outlines application procedures, EHD review and decision criteria, and appeal information for Applicants.

FGO 12/11/23 (jgr)

Summary:	This bill proposes to create a new ordinance entitled the “Environmental Protection Albuquerque-Bernalillo County Air Quality Control Board Environmental Justice in Air Quality Permitting Ordinance.” This Ordinance would be enforced by the City’s Environmental Health Department and would apply to “a person who intends to construct a new stationary source or modify an existing stationary source that is subject to permitting” under the New Mexico Administrative Code. 
Inclusive Community Engagement: 	The Ordinance would allow the imposition of “inclusive community engagement” on a permit applicant for the purpose of making it “possible for people with different abilities to fully participate, assuring that information is accessible and reaches populations in overburdened communities or vulnerable communities” as those communities are defined in the bill. The Ordinance would require that all persons have the opportunity to engage with meaningful involvement, which means that people have an opportunity to participate in decisions about activities that may affect their environment and/or health; the public’s contribution can influence the regulatory agency’s decision; community concerns will be considered in the decision-making process; and decision makers will seek out and facilitate the involvement of those potentially affected.
Mapping of Overburdened and Vulnerable Communities: 	This Ordinance would direct the Environmental Health Department to publish on its website a map of overburdened and vulnerable communities within 180 days of implementation of this Ordinance. Then, the requirements of this Ordinance will go into effect 180 calendar days after the map is published. The map shall include adverse environmental and public health indicators that have a demonstrable nexus with air pollution, but these indicators will not be considered standards required to identify quantities and duration of specified air contaminants that constitute air pollution. The Department shall attribute a value to each adverse environmental and public health indicator and may attribute a weight to each adverse environmental and public health indicator. For each adverse environmental and public health indicator, the Department shall provide in a publicly accessible manner the justification, literature, data source(s), methodology, and additional resources supporting inclusion of the adverse environmental and public health indicator on the map. Information regarding the adverse environmental and public health indicators used by the Department shall be based on the latest scientific data. Localized data may be used when it is peer reviewed, and consistent with accepted scientific practices. Recognized neighborhood associations may also submit information to be included with the map. This map will be updated following the US Census and notice shall be provided by the Department following any updates to the map. 
Pre-Application Environmental Justice Consultation:  	After the initial map goes into effect, potential applicants shall contact EHD for an environmental justice consultation before submitting any application. The consultation will be an opportunity for the potential applicant and EHD to discuss whether the potential applicant plans to locate the source or may potentially locate the source, in whole or in part, in an overburdened community or vulnerable community and what, if any, additional permitting requirements apply pursuant to this Ordinance before submitting an application to EHD.
Environmental Justice Assessment Report by Potential Applicants:	A potential applicant must conduct an environmental justice assessment and document its findings for the purpose of: providing the core information necessary to assess the existing adverse environmental and public health indicators in a vulnerable or overburdened community; document how the construction of a new stationary source or modification or relocation of an existing stationary source will impact those adverse environmental and public health indicators; any measures the source proposes to address those impacts; document the nature of the community it proposes to locate in; assess the source’s impact on the community; and provide the community with information about the source to facilitate meaningful public outreach. The report shall include twelve (12) components listed in the Ordinance. 
Enhanced Public Participation: Potential applicants must provide public notice, including a summary of the environmental justice assessment report and information about the circumstances in which a public information meeting may be held, if there is “significant public interest.” At the public information meeting, the potential applicant shall: (1) describe the source the potential applicant proposes to construct or modify; (2) provide a detailed presentation on the potential applicant’s environmental justice assessment report; (3) accept written and oral public comments, information, and questions; and (4) respond to comments and questions with sufficient detail. All expenses for the meeting will be paid for by the potential applicant. 
The Ordinance also outlines application procedures, EHD review and decision criteria, and appeal information for applicants.
Fiscal Impact: A FIA was not provided.
